**PostgreSQL sizing note: name length, column count and the connection limit**

This note covers three hard numbers from the official PostgreSQL documentation (current version) that matter when designing the schema and pool for the new service.

**Identifier length.** By default, a table, column or other identifier can be at most 63 bytes long. PostgreSQL uses at most `NAMEDATALEN` − 1 bytes of an identifier, and `NAMEDATALEN` defaults to 64. You can write longer names in commands, but PostgreSQL silently cuts them to 63 bytes. Raising the limit means changing `NAMEDATALEN` in `src/include/pg_config_manual.h` and recompiling (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limits appendix gives the same 63-byte figure (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). The limit is in bytes, not characters, so names with multi-byte UTF-8 characters run out sooner. Because longer names are cut silently, two long generated names (from an ORM or for constraints and indexes) can end up identical after truncation and collide. Keep names well under 63 bytes.

**Columns per table.** A table can have at most 1,600 columns. The docs add that the real ceiling is lower, because each row (tuple) must fit on a single page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). A web search also turned up a copy of the same appendix, which adds that dropped columns still count toward the limit. I only saw that point in the search results and did not open the page, so treat it as unconfirmed here. In practice, a wide table full of fixed-width columns will hit the page-size limit long before 1,600. If the design ever needs hundreds of columns, consider a JSONB column or splitting the data into related tables.

**max_connections default.** The documentation says "the default is typically 100 connections, but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). So 100 is the usual value, not a guarantee. Check the actual value on the target server with `SHOW max_connections;`. A few of those slots are reserved for superusers and replication, and managed services often set their own value. Each connection is a separate backend process with its own memory, so raising this number has a real cost.

**What this means for the service.** Add up every instance's pool, plus migration tools, cron jobs and admin sessions. With a default of around 100, a few app replicas with pools of 20–30 each will run out of connections quickly. A connection pooler such as PgBouncer is the usual fix when you need many client connections.

**Recommendation:** Keep identifiers short ASCII names well under 63 bytes, and keep tables far narrower than the 1,600-column limit so rows fit comfortably on a page. Size each app pool so that the total across all replicas, jobs and admin sessions stays below the server's actual `max_connections` (often 100), and put PgBouncer in front if you need more client connections than that.

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults on a fresh install**

The question was what a new PostgreSQL install uses for three memory and WAL settings before anyone changes them. I took all three answers from the current official PostgreSQL documentation.

**work_mem.** This setting caps how much memory one query operation can use, such as a sort or a hash table, before it starts writing temporary files to disk. The documentation says "The default value is four megabytes (`4MB`)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The limit applies to each operation, not to each session or query. A complex query can run several sorts and hashes at the same time, and many sessions can run at once, so the total memory used can be many times the setting. Raise it carefully and keep the number of connections in mind.

**shared_buffers.** This is the main shared memory area PostgreSQL uses to cache data pages. The documentation says "The default is typically 128 megabytes (`128MB`), but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). So on a fresh install, check the value you actually got with `SHOW shared_buffers;` rather than assuming 128MB. On a dedicated database server with a lot of RAM, 128MB is small. The usual starting point is a much larger share of system memory, and changing it requires a server restart.

**max_wal_size.** This is the amount of write-ahead log (WAL) that can build up before PostgreSQL forces a checkpoint. In the Checkpoints section, the documentation says "The default is 1 GB" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). It is a soft limit: under heavy load or if WAL archiving is failing, the WAL can grow past it. Under heavy write load, 1GB can cause checkpoints to be triggered by WAL volume much more often than `checkpoint_timeout` would trigger them. Each checkpoint adds I/O spikes and writes more full-page images. Unlike shared_buffers, this setting only needs a configuration reload, not a restart.

Overall, the defaults are cautious so that PostgreSQL will start on almost any machine, not tuned for a dedicated server: 4MB of work memory per operation, about 128MB of shared buffers, and 1GB of WAL between forced checkpoints. On anything beyond a small test box, all three are worth reviewing. The cost of changing each one differs: shared_buffers needs a restart, the other two only need a reload, and work_mem can also be set per session or per role.

**Recommendation:** Start by raising shared_buffers to a sensible share of the server's RAM and raising max_wal_size so checkpoints are mostly triggered by time; then check the logs for checkpoint warnings. Leave work_mem at the global default or raise it modestly, and increase it per role or session for reporting and analytics workloads, so that many connections cannot use up memory together.

{"answers": {"1": "4MB", "2": "128MB (typically; may be less if kernel settings don't support it)", "3": "1GB"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html"]}}

## Research note: DuckDB vs SQLite as an analytics side-store, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15

**Memory (DuckDB).** By default, DuckDB sets its `memory_limit` to 80% of the system's RAM. The Global Configuration Options table in its configuration docs lists this default (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). I first opened the "stable" docs URL, which only redirected to this 2.0 page (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/configuration/overview). This matters if DuckDB runs on the same host as PostgreSQL. Left at the default, a heavy analytical query could claim most of the machine's memory and compete with PostgreSQL's shared buffers and work memory. On a shared host, set `memory_limit` explicitly to a lower value, such as a fixed number of gigabytes, so the two engines don't starve each other.

**File size (SQLite).** SQLite's limits page says a database file can hold at most 4,294,967,294 pages. At the largest page size of 65,536 bytes, that comes to about 2.8e+14 bytes, which the page gives as 281 terabytes (256 tebibytes) (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). The same page notes that this upper bound is untested, because the developers don't have hardware that can reach it. In practice, file size won't be the limit for a side-store. The things that will matter are SQLite's row-oriented storage and single-writer design, which make large scans and aggregations slower than in a columnar engine like DuckDB.

**MERGE (PostgreSQL).** The MERGE command first shipped in PostgreSQL 15. The 15.0 release notes list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" in their overview. Under Utility Commands they add that it adjusts one table to match another and is "similar to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT but more batch-oriented" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/). So yes, MERGE is available on PostgreSQL 15. You can use it to apply batch upserts on the PostgreSQL side, for example when syncing summary tables computed in the side-store back into the main database. Older servers (14 and earlier) would need `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` instead.

**Putting it together.** Both engines are embedded and have no server to run, so the choice depends on the workload. If the side-store's job is analytical (scans, aggregations, joins over millions of rows, reading Parquet or CSV exports from PostgreSQL), DuckDB's columnar, vectorized engine fits better. Its main operational catch is the memory default described above. SQLite is better at small transactional lookups, embedding in an application, and long-term file stability. Its 281 TB ceiling is effectively unlimited, but it isn't built for analytical throughput.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB as the analytics side-store and set `memory_limit` explicitly below the 80%-of-RAM default whenever it shares a host with PostgreSQL. Write results back to PostgreSQL 15 with MERGE, which that version supports natively.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of RAM", "2": "about 281 TB", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/"]}}

**Research note: TLS 1.3, DNS label length and HTTP 418**

**1. TLS 1.3 specification.** TLS 1.3 was first specified in RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3". It was published in August 2018 as a Proposed Standard on the Internet Standards Track, and it obsoleted RFCs 5077, 5246 (TLS 1.2) and 6961 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). The RFC Editor page for RFC 8446 now marks it as obsolete and points to RFC 9846. RFC 9846 has the same title and is also a Proposed Standard. Its abstract says it "specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol". It is a minor revision that keeps the version number and stays backward compatible with RFC 8446. It obsoletes RFC 8446 and several older TLS 1.2-era documents, and it adds new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). The page I read showed only a 2026 copyright year, not a publication date. The guideline should therefore cite RFC 9846 as the current TLS 1.3 specification. Many vendor documents and existing policies still cite RFC 8446, so it is worth naming both: RFC 8446 as the original and RFC 9846 as the replacement. The wire protocol called "TLS 1.3" did not change.

**2. Maximum DNS label length.** RFC 1035, "Domain Names – Implementation and Specification", sets the size limits in Section 2.3.4. It says labels must be "63 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). A label is one dot-separated part of a host name, such as `www` in `www.example.com`. So no single part of a host name may be longer than 63 octets. The same section also limits the full name to 255 octets, which matters for long, deeply nested names. For internationalised names, the limit applies to the encoded (ASCII) form, not the characters a user sees, so a short-looking non-ASCII label can still exceed it.

**3. "I'm a teapot".** Status code 418, "I'm a teapot", comes from RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)", dated 1 April 1998. Section 2.3.2 states: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). RFC 2324 was an April Fools' document and extends the HTCPCP joke protocol, not HTTP itself. The guideline should therefore say that 418 is not a status code for real HTTP APIs and that services should not return it for real error conditions. Some frameworks and public sites do use it as an easter egg. I did not read the current HTTP semantics RFC on how 418 is treated in the HTTP status-code registry today, so this note makes no claim about that.

**Recommendation.** The guideline should require TLS 1.3 as specified in RFC 9846 (the successor to RFC 8446), validate every host-name label against the 63-octet limit in RFC 1035, and check the 255-octet limit on full names in the same place. It should also ban HTTP 418 from production APIs, because RFC 2324 defines it only as an April Fools' joke and clients cannot rely on it meaning anything.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446 (original TLS 1.3 spec; now obsoleted by RFC 9846, which also specifies TLS 1.3)", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418, defined in RFC 2324 (HTCPCP/1.0)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324"]}}

**Research note: timeout and network defaults for the deploy runbook**

**AWS Lambda timeout.** The Lambda timeout is the longest a function can run on one invocation. It defaults to 3 seconds and can be raised in 1-second steps up to 900 seconds (15 minutes). The console accepts any value from 1 to 900 seconds (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page has one exception. Functions on Lambda Managed Instances can run up to 5,400 seconds (90 minutes) for asynchronous invocations and most event source mapping invocations (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). For a standard function, the runbook should treat 900 seconds as the hard limit. You can set the timeout with `aws lambda update-function-configuration --timeout` or with the `Timeout` property in a SAM template.

**Kubernetes Pod termination grace period.** The Kubernetes Pod lifecycle page says a Pod "is granted a term to terminate gracefully, which defaults to 30 seconds." It also says "the default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). During that window the kubelet sends SIGTERM and lets the containers shut down. When the period runs out, any process still running is killed. If the service needs more time to drain connections or finish work, set `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in the Pod spec.

**Docker default bridge subnet.** The default bridge network (docker0) uses 172.17.0.0/16, with the gateway at 172.17.0.1. Docker's own bridge-driver page doesn't state this as a documented default. It shows it only in an example, where a container on the default bridge has the address `172.17.0.2/16` (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/). The `dockerd` reference describes the `--bip` and `--fixed-cidr` flags but gives no default value for them (source: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/dockerd/). A third-party lab guide shows `docker network inspect` output for the default bridge with `"Subnet": "172.17.0.0/16"` in its IPAM config (source: https://docker-k8s-lab.readthedocs.io/en/latest/docker/bridged-network.html). This value is the long-standing behaviour, but it is less firmly documented than the other two answers. It can be changed with `bip` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`, which matters on machines where 172.17.0.0/16 clashes with a VPN or corporate network. To be sure on a given host, run `docker network inspect bridge`.

**Recommendation.** Set the application's shutdown and drain timeouts below each platform's limit: well under 900 seconds on Lambda, and below `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` on Kubernetes, raising that above the 30-second default if the service needs it. For local Docker, have the runbook check the bridge subnet with `docker network inspect bridge` instead of assuming 172.17.0.0/16, and set `bip` wherever that range clashes with existing networks.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"], "3": ["https://docker-k8s-lab.readthedocs.io/en/latest/docker/bridged-network.html", "https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/"]}}

**Research note: defaults for test and tooling configuration**

This note covers three defaults that matter when setting up the repository's test and tooling settings. Each one was checked against official documentation or a primary source in this session.

**Vitest per-test timeout.** Vitest's `testTimeout` option defaults to 5,000 ms in Node.js. When browser mode is on (`browser.enabled` is true), the default rises to 15,000 ms, and setting the option to `0` turns the timeout off (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). Five seconds is usually plenty for unit tests. Integration tests that start containers, run database migrations or make network calls often go over it, though. It is better to raise the limit for those suites on purpose than to raise it everywhere.

**First Linux kernel with Rust in mainline.** Linux 6.1 was the first mainline kernel with Rust language support. The KernelNewbies summary of that release says: "This release adds support for the Rust programming language." It adds that this is "some initial support for Rust, which will be improved in later releases" (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). So 6.1 is only the earliest kernel with any Rust support. The Rust abstractions available for writing real drivers have grown a lot in later releases. If the team builds Rust kernel code, it should choose a recent kernel, ideally a long-term support (LTS) release, rather than 6.1 itself. I read the first part of the KernelNewbies page, which contains this statement, not the whole page. I also did not check the kernel's own Rust documentation.

**PostgreSQL statement_timeout.** The default value of `statement_timeout` is 0, which means no timeout at all. The PostgreSQL documentation says: "A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). With the stock configuration, a runaway query can run forever and keep its locks and connection the whole time. That is rarely what an application or a test suite wants. The setting can be applied per role, per database, per session or per transaction, so we can set a limit for the application's role without affecting maintenance jobs. The same documentation page advises against setting it in `postgresql.conf`, because the limit would then apply to every session.

**Recommendation.** Keep Vitest's 5,000 ms default for unit tests, and set a longer timeout only for integration suites. Set Rust kernel work against a recent LTS kernel rather than 6.1, and set `statement_timeout` for the application role (for example, `ALTER ROLE app SET statement_timeout = '30s'`) instead of leaving the unlimited default.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms in browser mode)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
